Below is a concise, evidence-backed synthesis of how doping and related substitutions affect the electrochemical performance of 1T‑MoS2 across supercapacitors, hydrogen evolution electrocatalysis, and Zn‑ion batteries, including mechanisms and quantitative trends.

Summary
- Doping heteroatoms (N, O, halides) and transition metals (V, Cr, Ni, Co, Cu, Mn, Fe) into MoS2 systematically increases conductivity, tunes surface and basal-plane electronic structure, exposes edge planes, and can stabilize or enrich the metallic 1T phase, yielding improved kinetics and stability in both catalysis and energy storage. <cite id="98dc0884-0">The properties of 1T‑MoS2 can be greatly modified by different atoms/ions doping; Ni/O co-doping of NiO@1T‑MoS2/CFP improved HER activity, with Ni@1T‑MoS2 showing η50=187 mV and stable performance for ~28 hours, attributed to enhanced conductivity, active-site increase, and surface electron-density regulation</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-3">Metal doping (Zn, Co, Ni, Ce) adjusts Mo sites’ electronic structure to promote HER; e.g., Ni-doped MoS2 reached η=88 mV at 10 mA cm−2, and Ce-doped MoS2 achieved η=113.78 mV with enhanced defect-rich active sites</cite>.

1T‑MoS2 doping for hydrogen evolution (HER): mechanisms and performance
- Conductivity and active-site modulation: <cite id="98dc0884-0">Ni doping of 1T‑MoS2 increased conductivity and regulated electron density, creating more active sites and lowering overpotential (η50=187 mV) with stable HER for ~28 h</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-4">Ni-doped stabilized 1T/2H‑MoS2 formed Ni–S covalent bonds that induce S‑atom slip, stabilizing the 1T structure; the material delivered η=162 mV and a Tafel slope of 80 mV dec−1 with good stability</cite>. 
- Optimal dopant concentration matters: <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">V-doped MoS2 films showed progressively lower Tafel slopes (164.08 → 136.4 → 128.16 → 116.65 mV dec−1) and higher activity as V content increased from 25% to 33.3%, combining improved conductivity with enhanced edge accessibility; V-doped MoS2 outperformed both undoped 2H and 1T MoS2 in chemical stability, conductivity, and catalytic performance</cite>. <cite id="9fd8f38a-2">Quantitatively, overpotentials at 10 mA cm−2 decreased from 572.18 mV (intrinsic) to 465.18 mV (33.3% V-doped), with >90% activity retained after 9000 s; lowered Tafel slopes (116.65 mV dec−1) indicate improved kinetics</cite>. 
- Interface and heterostructure engineering with dopants: <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">A 1T‑MoS2/NiS interface exhibited the lowest Tafel slope (69 mV dec−1), a charge-transfer resistance ~0.4 Ω (vs ~2.9 Ω for 1T‑MoS2 alone), and maintained stability under chronoamperometry with slight degradation at −0.12 V; DFT analysis supported enhanced charge transfer and improved HER mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="9fd8f38a-4">The same heterostructure showed small Rct and stable high-current-density operation, attributing gains to strong NiS–1T‑MoS2 coupling</cite>. 
- Electron-donor/acceptor dopants tune adsorption energetics: <cite id="9fd8f38a-2">Cr-doped MoS2 achieved η=142 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and a Tafel slope of 61 mV dec−1 versus 206 mV and 85 mV dec−1 for pristine MoS2, indicating optimized hydrogen adsorption and faster kinetics via charge redistribution</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-3">N-doping produced S defects, exposed Mo sites, adjusted S-electron density, and activated S atoms as active sites, lowering η to 168 mV at 10 mA cm−2</cite>. 
- Phase and structural stabilization by dopants: <cite id="98dc0884-1">Co/Ni co-doping provided abundant electrons to Mo atoms, facilitating a phase transition to 1T‑MoS2 with excellent alkaline HER properties; Se and O co-insertion also drove 2H→1T transition; S-vacancy 1T‑MoS2 prepared via K intercalation and etching showed η=158 mV at 10 mA cm−2, Rct≈74.5 mV dec−1, and good stability, with charge-redistribution to Mo–Mo bonds improving ΔGH* for HER</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-0">Ni@1T‑MoS2’s superior activity was linked to increased active sites and optimized electron density</cite>. 
- Thermodynamic trade-offs: <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">While 1T‑MoS2 is more conductive and catalytically active than 2H‑MoS2, it is less thermodynamically stable; V-doping is proposed to combine chemical stability with high conductivity and excellent catalytic performance</cite>. 

1T‑MoS2 for supercapacitors: doping, phase enrichment, and intercalation/functionalization
- Metallic 1T phase boosts capacitance and rate: <cite id="b2a3e3f5-0">Exfoliated ultrathin ~100% 1T‑MoS2 showed σ=140 S m−1, 420 F g−1 capacitance, high surface area (67 m2 g−1), and good flexibility, indicating strong supercapacitor potential</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-4">Synthesis route controls phase and morphology; HT-grown MoS2 partially enriched in 1T delivered 466.66 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and retained capacity over 2000 cycles, outperforming CVD-grown 2H‑MoS2 (371.10 F g−1; 57.69 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1)</cite>. 
- 1T–2H hybridization and doping co-optimization: <cite id="b2a3e3f5-1">Increasing in-plane 1T fraction (2%→60%) by low-temperature annealing of exfoliated MoS2 monolayers raised capacitance to 366.9 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, with Rct≈0.68 kΩ sq−1 and 92.2% retention after 1000 cycles</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-3">Alkali intercalation, strain, or Re/Tc/Mn doping can drive 2H→1T transitions, increasing conductivity and improving supercapacitor performance; reviews emphasize that intrinsic and extrinsic modifications (phase engineering and composites) both enhance charge-storage</cite>. 
- Intercalation/functionalization as “doping-like” strategies: <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">Ammonium-intercalated MoS2 with significant 1T content showed 228 F g−1 at 5 mV s−1 and retained 127 F g−1 at 80 mV s−1; functionalizing 1T‑MoS2 with NH2Ph rings (Fc‑1T‑MoS2) raised specific capacitance to 501 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 with 76.32% retention after 2000 cycles, 2.6× higher than bare 1T‑MoS2, reflecting faster charge transport due to improved charge density/electronic properties</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-0">S-vacancy and K+-assisted strategies have also been shown to create conductive 1T networks and improve electrochemical activity</cite>. 
- Comparative context: <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">A-MoS2 (1T-rich) showed notable capacitance and retention, while Pt@1T/2H‑MoS2 composites enhanced specific capacitance and coulombic efficiency in cycling; 2H‑MoS2 alone (115.42 F g−1 at 10 mV s−1; 57.69 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1) lagged behind 1T-enriched variants, underscoring the benefit of metallic-phase enrichment</cite>. 

Doping for Zn‑ion batteries (AZIBs) and energy storage trade-offs
- 1T vs 2H in AZIBs: <cite id="98dc0884-2">Metallic 1T‑MoS2 exhibits better conductivity than semiconducting 2H; Shuang Gao synthesized 1T‑MoS2 with 0.95 nm interlayer spacing (vs 0.62 nm for 2H) as a cathode delivering 226.2 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g−1 and ~500 cycles at 1 A g−1; strong electrostatic attraction between framework and Zn2+ limits capacity</cite>. 
- Doping to improve kinetics and stability: <cite id="98dc0884-2">Doping and hybridization with conductive substrates can enhance conductivity, structural stability, and defect density; Mn was chosen as a case study for capacity and charge/discharge efficiency improvement in AZIBs</cite>. 
- Buffering ion–lattice interactions and spacing: <cite id="98dc0884-2">Increasing interlayer spacing mitigates Zn2+ trapping but weakens van der Waals forces and risks structural collapse; doping provides an alternative pathway to improve electrical transport and defect-controlled redox while balancing stability</cite>. 

Practical guidance: dopant choices, mechanisms, and design rules
- Dopant classes and effects:
  - Transition-metal dopants (Ni, Co, Cr, V): <cite id="98dc0884-0">Ni doping improves conductivity and active-site density, reducing η and stabilizing performance</cite>; <cite id="98dc0884-1">Co/Ni co-doping drives 2H→1T transition via electron enrichment of Mo and yields strong HER</cite>; <cite id="9fd8f38a-2">Cr-doping lowers η to 142 mV at 10 mA cm−2 with Tafel 61 mV dec−1 through charge redistribution and optimized adsorption</cite>; <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">V-doping reduces Tafel slopes and overpotentials, improving conductivity and exposing active sites, combining stability and kinetics</cite>. 
  - Heteroatom dopants (N, O, F, halides): <cite id="98dc0884-3">N-doping introduces S-vacancies/defects, activates S sites, lowers η to 168 mV</cite>; <cite id="98dc0884-1">O and Se co-insertion induces 2H→1T and improves HER with η=158 mV and Tafel 74.5 mV dec−1</cite>; <cite id="98dc0884-3">F-doping can control active sites via plasma etching</cite>. 
  - Interface/hybrid dopants: <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">NiS coupling to 1T‑MoS2 lowers Rct to ~0.4 Ω and Tafel to 69 mV dec−1, improving charge transfer and stability</cite>. 
- Mechanisms consistent across systems:
  - Electronic structure tuning and conductivity: <cite id="98dc0884-0">Dopants increase carrier density and reduce contact resistance, enhancing HER kinetics</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">Functionalization and intercalation increase charge density and accelerate charge storage, raising capacitance and cycling stability</cite>. 
  - Defect/edge exposure and active-site density: <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">Dopants (e.g., V) add basal-plane active sites and improve edge accessibility, lowering Tafel slopes</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-3">N-doping generates S-vacancies and exposes Mo sites, activating S atoms</cite>. 
  - Phase stabilization and pseudocapacitive redox: <cite id="98dc0884-1">Metal co-doping and anion insertion promote 1T formation and charge redistribution (e.g., Mo–Mo activation), improving catalytic intermediates’ free energy</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-3">Re/Tc/Mn doping and alkali intercalation induce 2H→1T with higher conductivity and capacitance</cite>. 
- Design trade-offs and mitigation:
  - Thermodynamic stability of 1T and interfacial contact: <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">1T is less thermodynamically stable than 2H; optimal donor dopants (V, Cr) combine stability with conductivity</cite>. <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">Strong interfacial coupling (NiS) reduces Rct and enhances durability</cite>. 
  - Structural integrity under cycling: <cite id="98dc0884-2">Doping improves conductivity and defect density but must be balanced with interlayer spacing and mechanical robustness to avoid collapse during Zn2+ insertion/extraction</cite>. 
  - Over-oxidation and phase loss: <cite id="98dc0884-1">S-vacancy creation and intercalant extraction require careful redox control to preserve 1T network</cite>. 

Comparative baselines and benchmarks
- Baseline phases and undoped MoS2: <cite id="9fd8f38a-0">Intrinsic 2H‑MoS2 is stable but has high overpotential and large Tafel slopes; 1T‑MoS2 improves conductivity and activity but needs stabilization</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">2H‑MoS2 at 10 mV s−1 shows 115.42 F g−1 and 57.69 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1, significantly below 1T-enriched variants</cite>. 
- Doped/modified 1T‑MoS2 highlights:
  - HER: <cite id="98dc0884-0">Ni@1T‑MoS2 η50=187 mV with long stability</cite>; <cite id="9fd8f38a-2">V-doped 33.3% films reach η=465.18 mV vs intrinsic 572.18 mV at 10 mA cm−2</cite>; <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">1T‑MoS2/NiS Tafel=69 mV dec−1, Rct=0.4 Ω</cite>. 
  - Supercapacitors: <cite id="b2a3e3f5-0">1T‑MoS2 420 F g−1 with σ=140 S m−1</cite>; <cite id="b2a3e3f5-1">40% 1T hybrid monolayers 366.9 F g−1 with ~0.68 kΩ Rct and 92.2% retention after 1000 cycles</cite>; <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">Fc‑1T‑MoS2 501 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 with 2000‑cycle retention</cite>; <cite id="b2a3e3f5-4">HT‑MoS2 (1T-enriched) 466.66 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 and 2000‑cycle stability</cite>. 
  - Zn‑ion batteries: <cite id="98dc0884-2">1T‑MoS2 with 0.95 nm spacing delivered 226.2 mAh g−1 at 0.1 A g−1 and ~500 cycles at 1 A g−1; Mn doping investigated to elevate capacity and efficiency</cite>. 

Takeaways and how to apply doping to 1T‑MoS2
- Choose dopants and architectures to jointly maximize conductivity, active-site density, and phase stability. <cite id="98dc0884-0">Electron-donor dopants like Ni can simultaneously enhance conductivity and regulate surface electron density to boost HER</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-1">Co/Ni co-doping can trigger 2H→1T transitions and improve alkaline HER via electron-rich Mo sites and S‑vacancy activation</cite>. <cite id="9fd8f38a-2">Cr and V dopants improve adsorption energetics and kinetics, lowering overpotentials and Tafel slopes</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-3">N and F heteroatom doping introduce vacancies/defects and control site selectivity, activating S/Mo and improving HER</cite>. 
- For supercapacitors, favor 1T-enriched or 1T–2H hybrid structures with conductive scaffolds and “doping-like” intercalation/functionalization to increase redox pseudocapacitance and power. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-1">Raising 1T fraction to ~40–60% boosted capacitance and reduced resistance</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">Ammonium intercalation and NH2Ph functionalization increased capacitance and cycling stability by improving charge transport and storage</cite>. 
- Mitigate trade-offs by coupling dopants with interface engineering and mechanical buffering. <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">NiS coupling to 1T‑MoS2 minimizes charge-transfer losses and stabilizes kinetics</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-2">In AZIBs, balance interlayer spacing with doping to limit Zn2+ trapping and maintain structural integrity</cite>. 
- Monitor dopant-induced phase drift and over-oxidation. <cite id="98dc0884-1">Se/O insertion and S‑vacancy creation require careful redox control to preserve the 1T network and active sites</cite>. 

Limitations and open questions
- While multiple dopants consistently improve kinetics and stability, optimal concentrations and synergistic co-doping strategies remain system-specific; for example, HER activity and stability depend on dopant concentration and support choice, with Ni-doped MoS2 achieving η≈150–187 mV and Tafel≈63–85 mV dec−1 depending on interface and phase state. <cite id="98dc0884-0">Ni@1T‑MoS2 achieved η50=187 mV with long stability and lower Tafel than pristine</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-3">Ni-doped nanosheets reached η=88 mV at 10 mA cm−2</cite>. <cite id="9fd8f38a-1">1T‑MoS2/NiS achieved Tafel=69 mV dec−1 and Rct≈0.4 Ω</cite>. 
- For OER/ORR, direct evidence on doped 1T‑MoS2 is less abundant in the retrieved set; analogous HER mechanisms (electronic modulation, edge exposure, and heterostructure coupling) plausibly translate, but targeted benchmarking against standard OER catalysts would clarify absolute activity and durability. <cite id="98dc0884-1">Phase transition and defect engineering strategies validated for HER suggest analogous pathways for OER via 1T enrichment and dopant-induced charge redistribution</cite>. 
- Bottom line: Doping 1T‑MoS2 with transition metals or heteroatoms—often in conjunction with interfacial coupling and controlled defect/vacancy engineering—reliably enhances electrochemical performance by improving conductivity, activating additional catalytic sites, and stabilizing the metallic 1T phase; the magnitude and durability of gains depend on dopant identity, concentration, and composite architecture. <cite id="98dc0884-0">Doping can markedly modify 1T‑MoS2 electronic structure and active sites, improving HER activity and stability</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-1">Co/Ni dopants and anion co-insertion drive 2H→1T and improve catalytic descriptors</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-0">1T‑MoS2 can reach 420 F g−1 in supercapacitors when ultrathin and highly conductive</cite>. <cite id="b2a3e3f5-2">Interface/functionalization strategies push specific capacitance toward 500 F g−1 with long-life cycling</cite>. <cite id="98dc0884-2">In Zn‑ion batteries, 1T‑MoS2 with controlled spacing and Mn doping supports high capacity and long cycles</cite>.

Title: Scaling up Simultaneous Exfoliation and 2H to 1T Phase Transformation of MoS2
Snippet: Large‐scale production of high‐quality ultrathin layers (1–3 nm) of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) with absolute (≈100%) 1T‐phase is still in its infancy. Therefore, it is extremely crucial to have a technique for the mass production of ultrathin 1T‐MoS2 layers. Here, a direct, single‐step, and ultra‐fast technique that produces high‐quality ultrathin layers of 1T‐MoS2 with a production rate as high as 58 g h−1 without the usage of any intercalates or solvents is demonstrated. The exfoliated ultrathin 1T‐MoS2 layers exhibited ≈100% 1T‐phase with a large specific surface area (67 m2 g−1), higher electrical conductivity (140 S m−1), high thermal stability (up to 500 °C) and hydrophilicity (water contact angle (WCA): ≈23.4⁰). The ultrathin 1T‐MoS2 layers showed a higher specific capacitance of 420 F g−1; perhaps an ideal candidate for the electrodes of supercapacitors. Moreover, the ultrathin 1T‐MoS2 layer exhibited better mechanical flexibility and retained its original performance on bending between 0 and 180⁰ angles. Further, to assess the adeptness of the protocol, An initial trial is done on other transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) i.e., tungsten disulfide (WS2), and observe similar results. The work sheds light on the simultaneous exfoliation and phase transformation of TMDs in large quantities, and detailed proofs‐of‐concept demonstrate its application in next‐generation energy storage devices.

Title: Structural phases and electrochemical properties of 2D MoS2 for supercapacitor applications
Snippet: Supercapacitors (SCs) are becoming popular as electrochemical energy storage devices because they have a high-power density, fast charge and discharge rates, and good cycling stability. The materials used in the electrodes have a big effect on how well supercapacitors work overall. Two-dimensional molybdenum disulfide (2D MoS2) has gotten a lot of attention among a number of other electrode materials, such as carbon-based materials, metal oxides, and conducting polymers. This is mostly because of its layered structure, large surface area, and ability to change its electrical properties. MoS2 shows strong links between structure and properties. The bulk form of MoS2 has an indirect bandgap of about 1.2 eV, while the monolayer form has a direct bandgap of about 1.8 eV. This difference in bandgap affects how well it works in optoelectronic and electrochemical applications. MoS2 also comes in different forms, such as the semiconducting 2H, the metallic 1T, and the rarer 3R. Each of these has its own unique atomic structure. Alkali metal intercalation, mechanical strain, or doping with elements like Re, Tc, or Mn can cause phase changes from 2H to 1T. This makes the material more conductive and improves the performance of supercapacitors. This review thoroughly examines recent advancements in phase engineering and the electrochemical performance of 2D MoS2-based supercapacitor electrodes, highlighting the effects of intrinsic modifications (phase engineering) and extrinsic modifications (composite formation) on the charge-storage characteristics of MoS2.

Title: Enhancing the supercapacitor performance of MoS2 nanostructures through metallic phase enrichment and morphology control
Snippet: Abstract Molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) has attracted considerable attention as a promising electrode material for supercapacitor applications due to its tunable electronic structure and layered morphology. However, its electrochemical performance is highly dependent on the synthesis route and the resulting structural characteristics. In this study, MoS2 nanostructures were synthesized using two distinct methods, hydrothermal synthesis (HT) and chemical vapor deposition (CVD), yielding materials with markedly different morphologies, particle sizes, and phase compositions. The HT method produced nanoscale MoS2 with partial enrichment of the metallic 1T phase, while the CVD approach yielded highly crystalline, few-layer 2H-MoS2 nanosheets. Electrodes were fabricated on nickel foam current collectors, whose three-dimensional porous architecture facilitated efficient charge transport and electrolyte accessibility. Electrochemical evaluation revealed that HT-MoS2 exhibits superior supercapacitive performance, delivering a high specific capacitance of 466.66 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1, compared to 371.10 F g−1 for CVD-MoS2. In addition, the HT-MoS2 electrode demonstrated excellent galvanostatic charge–discharge behavior and retained high capacitance stability over 2,000 charge–discharge cycles. These results highlight the critical role of synthesis-driven phase and morphology engineering, as well as electrode architecture, in optimizing the supercapacitor performance of MoS2-based materials and highlight their potential for advanced energy storage applications.

Title: Recent progress of MoS2 for photocatalytic and electrocatalytic hydrogen generation—A review
Snippet: Recently, atom intercalation in MoS2 has been confirmed to stabilize MoS2's phase structure. For instance, Ekspong et al. [91] developed sulfur-rich intercalated 1T-MoS2 on graphitic nanoribbons with an S:Mo ratio of ~2.3:1, which sustained its stability for several months. Both experimental and theoretical results found that the active sites on the basal planes were activated with an outstanding ∆GH value of 0.06 eV, which in turn improved catalytic activity. Gao's group [92] confirmed that the formation of 1T-MoS2 can be induced using metal doping. Their results found that Co/Ni co-doping provided abundant electrons for Mo atoms, subsequently leading to phase transition. The obtained Co/Ni-MoS2 possessed an excellent alkaline HER property. Jiang et al. [93] proposed a strategy of Se and O co-insertion to induce the transition of MoS2 from the 2H phase to the 1T phase. Guo's group [94] reported a chemical etching method to construct 1T-MoS2 with S vacancies (1T-MoS2-VS) for efficient catalytic HER. Figure 14(a) shows the schematic of the synthesis of 1T-MoS2-VS. K + ions intercalated in the interlayer of 2H-MoS2 to form KMoS2, and 1T-MoS2 was obtained by the extraction of K + from KMoS2. Afterward, the 1T-MoS2 was immersed in an acidic K2Cr2O7 solution to obtain S vacancies. The electrochemical measurements are shown in Figure 14(b-d). The 1T-MoS2-VS exhibited a lower overpotential of 158 mV at 10 mA•cm −2 and a smaller Tafel slope of 74.5 mV•dec −1 . A little degradation in its current density after a continuous 24-h test suggested remarkable stability for HER. Particularly, the electronic states of the 1T-MoS2-VS (Figure 14(e-g)) demonstrated the charge redistribution with the activated Mo-Mo bonds, which led to an optimal ΔGH* value for catalytic HER.

Title: Effect of manganese doping on the electrochemical performance of MoS2 as a cathode material for rechargeable Zn-ion batteries
Snippet: For instance, metallic 1T-MoS2 boasts better conductivity than its semiconducting 2H counterpart. While 1T-MoS2 shows superior electrochemical performance, its limited zinc storage sites restrict its capacity due to strong electrostatic attraction between the framework and inserted Zn²⁺ ions, hindering further ion insertion [9]. Increasing interlayer spacing is a common approach to mitigate this interaction [10][11]. However, this weakens the van der Waals forces between MoS2 layers, compromising structural stability [9]. Shuang Gao et al. synthesized 1T-MoS2 with a 0.95 nm interlayer spacing (versus 0.62 nm for 2H-MoS2), which when applied as cathode material delivered a high capacity of 226.2 mAh/g at 0.1 A/g, maintaining stability for roughly 500 cycles at 1 A/g [13]. To improve the performance of MoS2 cathodes for AZIBs batteries and enable practical applications, we need to explore other strategies for enhancing their specific capacity and charge/discharge efficiency. Doping with heteroatoms or hybridizing with conductive subtracts can improve the electrical conductivity, structural stability, and defect density of MoS2 materials [9,11], but these strategies remain less studied. 

In this study, we synthesized MoS2 material doped with Mn atoms in different molar ratio by hydrothermal method and then studied the effect of this doping on the specific capacity and charge/discharge efficiency of MoS2 when applied as a cathode for AZIBs. Mn was chosen because it is an abundant element, less toxic and less studied.

Title: Recent progress of MoS2 for photocatalytic and electrocatalytic hydrogen generation—A review
Snippet: In electrocatalysis, element doping has been deemed to be an effective to regulate active sites of catalysts for various reactions. Element doping comprises two types: metal doping and heteroatom doping (nonmetal doping). Metal doping (e.g., Zn, Co, Ni, etc.) [110][111][112][113] can effectively adjust the electronic structure of Mo sites in MoS2 to promote high HER performance. For instance, Xu et al. [110] proposed transition metal Zn doping of MoS2 to engineer its energy level for efficient HER. They found that Zn doping provided an energy level matching the HER's kinetic acceleration, resulting in a superior electrochemical HER activity. Xue et al. [112] developed ultra-small Ni-doped MoS2 nanosheets on hollow carbon microtubes. The results confirmed that moderate Ni doping tuned the electronic structure of active sites in MoS2. As a result, the obtained catalyst exhibited excellent activity with enhanced HER kinetics, requiring a low overpotential of 88 mV at 10 mA•cm −2 and demonstrating better stability in 0.5M H2SO4. Kong et al. [114] used rare earth Ce for a doping strategy to prepare Ce-doped MoS2. The Ce-doped MoS2 was rich in defects and regulated the electronic structure, further promoting HER performance with a small overpotential of 113.78 mV. 

Heteroatom doping (N, F, P, etc.) [115][116][117][118][119] for enhancing catalytic HER has also received great attention. Li et al. reported N-doped MoS2, fabricated via a simple one-step hydrothermal strategy, as an efficient HER catalyst [115]. The N doping produced rich S defects to expose Mo sites and adjust the electron density of S atoms to activate S atoms as active sites. The N-doped MoS2 revealed a much lower overpotential of 168 mV at 10 mA•cm −2 than that of pure MoS2. Zhang et al. [118] developed F-doped MoS2 with controllable active sites by using a plasma etching strategy.

Title: Metal-semiconductor 1T/2H-MoS2 by a heteroatom-doping strategy for enhanced electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution
Snippet: Abstract Complicated synthesis procedure and instability of 1T-MoS2 impede its practical application for hydrogen evolution reaction. Here, we propose a new strategy to drive the synthesis of stabilized 1T-MoS2 by Ni doping. Ni doping forms the Ni S covalent bonds, inducing the slip of S atoms and stabilizing 1T structure. The materials were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy. Electrochemical tests including linear sweep voltammetry etc. indicate that the 1T/2H-MoS2/8%Ni has an overpotential of 162 mV and a Tafel slope of 80 mV dec−1 along with a good stability.

Title: Structural phases and electrochemical properties of 2D MoS2 for supercapacitor applications
Snippet: Supercapacitors (SCs) are becoming popular as electrochemical energy storage devices because they have a high-power density, fast charge and discharge rates, and good cycling stability. The materials used in the electrodes have a big effect on how well supercapacitors work overall. Two-dimensional molybdenum disulfide (2D MoS2) has gotten a lot of attention among a number of other electrode materials, such as carbon-based materials, metal oxides, and conducting polymers. This is mostly because of its layered structure, large surface area, and ability to change its electrical properties. MoS2 shows strong links between structure and properties. The bulk form of MoS2 has an indirect bandgap of about 1.2 eV, while the monolayer form has a direct bandgap of about 1.8 eV. This difference in bandgap affects how well it works in optoelectronic and electrochemical applications. MoS2 also comes in different forms, such as the semiconducting 2H, the metallic 1T, and the rarer 3R. Each of these has its own unique atomic structure. Alkali metal intercalation, mechanical strain, or doping with elements like Re, Tc, or Mn can cause phase changes from 2H to 1T. This makes the material more conductive and improves the performance of supercapacitors. This review thoroughly examines recent advancements in phase engineering and the electrochemical performance of 2D MoS2-based supercapacitor electrodes, highlighting the effects of intrinsic modifications (phase engineering) and extrinsic modifications (composite formation) on the charge-storage characteristics of MoS2.

Title: Enhancing the supercapacitor performance of MoS2 nanostructures through metallic phase enrichment and morphology control
Snippet: Abstract Molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) has attracted considerable attention as a promising electrode material for supercapacitor applications due to its tunable electronic structure and layered morphology. The HT method produced nanoscale MoS2 with partial enrichment of the metallic 1T phase, while the CVD approach yielded highly crystalline, few-layer 2H-MoS2 nanosheets. Title: The effects of polymorphism and lithium intercalation on the hydrogen evolution reaction for the basal planes of MoS2.
Snippet: The activity of Li-intercalated MoS2 phases for the hydrogen evolution reaction is investigated using density functional theory. The most stable semiconducting 2H phase, the metallic 1T' phase, and a polymorphous surface composed of alternating H and T' phases (1T″) are investigated. The local structure of the MoS2 surface is found to define its reactivity. In all cases, active sites for the hydrogen evolution process are restricted to T-like sulphur sites. Li-intercalation is found to promote hydrogen evolution reaction reactivity for the H phase whilst having little effect on the T phase. While improved compared to the non-intercalated phase, the Li-intercalated H phase MoS2 still has minimal activity for the hydrogen evolution reaction. The same effect of intercalation is also found for another transition metal dichalcogenide, MoSe2. The ability to improve reactivity in this way makes ion intercalation a promising space for designing new 2D catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction.
</snippet>

Title: Operando Insights on the Degradation Mechanisms of Rhenium-doped and Undoped Molybdenum Disulfide Nanocatalysts for Electrolyzer Applications
Snippet: Molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) is widely regarded as a Pt alternative for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic media due to its high catalytic activity, abundance and low price [1][2][3].However, it crystallizes in the thermodynamically stable 2H-MoS2 polytype, which only possesses high HER activity on the edge sites [4].In order to enhance the HER performance of MoS2, exposure of the edge active sites can be maximized in nanostructures [5] e.g. with a nanoflower morphology [6,7].Other strategies to optimize the HER activity include sulfur-defect engineering [8,9], phase engineering [10,11], the use of amorphous MoS2 layers [12] or doping with transition metals [13,14].

In particular, Re-doped MoS2 nanomaterials (RexMo1-xS2) have shown remarkable improvement on the HER activity over MoS2 nanocatalysts [15][16][17][18].The n-type Re dopant not only acts as an electron donor, but also favors local transformation to 1T-MoS2, while both effects contribute to improved HER performance [19][20][21][22].Although the 1T-MoS2 polytype provides enhanced conductivity and basal-plane HER active sites [11,23], it is a metastable phase which can revert to the 2H phase.Nevertheless, Re-doping stabilizes the 1T phase and 1T-RexMo1-xS2 has shown long lifetimes on the shelf and stability under HER conditions [15,17].In comparison, alkali metals can also stabilize 1T-MoS2 nanocatalysts, but they are known to suffer from poor durability [22,24].Indeed, beyond the HER activity, the appeal of MoS2-based nanocatalysts relies on the high stability during operation.

Title: Ru-Doped Induced Phase Engineering of MoS2 for Boosting Electrocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
Snippet: Moreover, phase junctions within the same materials have been demonstrated as a promising approach due to the unique benefits of robust coupling, high electron affinity, and the absence of foreign elements. For instance, Cai and coworkers demonstrated that the incorporation of 25% 1T-MoS 2 into 2H-MoS 2 nanosheets resulted in a ten-fold increase in electron concentration [27]. Most recently, we have reported a significant enhancement in photocatalytic hydrogen evolution through improving the conductivity of ZnIn 2 S 4 by the incorporation of the 2H@1T-MoS 2 phase [28]. However, the mechanism of the MoS 2 transformation from 2H to 1T is still unclear, and the influence of the phase transformation of MoS 2 on the HER activity also requires in-depth research. 

Ruthenium (Ru) doping has been reported to promote the phase transformation of MoS 2 from 2H to 1T and shows the high HER activity. Moreover, the bond energy of Ru-H is approximately 65 kcal mol −1 , equivalent to the energy of Pt-H bond [29][30][31]. In previous studies, Ru materials including single atoms, nanoparticles, and clusters, have been demonstrated to possess high HER performances [32][33][34][35]. Zhang et al. have reported that MoS 2 -based electrocatalysts loaded with the single-atom Ru exhibit the significantly enhanced HER activity due to the 2H-to-1T phase transition [36]. The reason for phase transition is owing to the introduction of sulfur vacancies by Ru single-atom doping. Recently, Wang and co-workers believed that single-atom Ru substitution for the Mo atom in MoS 2 resulted in the 2H-to-1T phase transition, which makes the Ru-MoS 2 electrocatalysts have superb HER performances [37]. However, there is still controversy over the mechanism of the MoS 2 transformation from 2H to 1T through the introduction of Ru. It is necessary to reveal the mechanism through the combination of theoretical calculation and experimental study. 

In this work, we employed the DFT calculation and experiments to study the electrocatalytic HER activity on Ru-doped MoS 2 catalysts.

Summary
Across hydrogen-evolution catalysts based on 1T‑MoS2, transition‑metal doping causally improves electrochemical performance primarily by stabilizing the 1T polytype against reversion to 2H, which unlocks downstream electronic‑structure and defect changes (electron doping, basal‑plane active sites, optimized adsorption thermodynamics) that together raise conductivity, active‑site density, and durability under HER conditions. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Doping transition‑metal ions onto 1T‑MoS2 lowers overpotentials and improves stability, with Ni outperforming Co/Fe/Cu/Mn in a controlled ion‑modification study, and the authors attribute gains to enhanced conductivity, increased active sites, and regulated surface electron density</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Reviews summarizing atom intercalation and metal doping report that Co/Ni co‑doping induces the 1T phase and that S‑vacancy engineering and 1T stabilization strategies yield lower overpotentials and improved Tafel slopes with optimized ΔGH* values</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-3">Direct mechanistic evidence shows Ni forms Ni–S covalent bonds that induce sulfur slip and stabilize the 1T structure, delivering overpotential of 162 mV and Tafel slope of 80 mV dec−1 with good stability</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Operando studies of rhenium doped MoS2 show Re acts as an n‑type donor and favors local transformation to 1T, stabilizing the 1T phase and enabling long shelf and HER lifetimes; 1T provides enhanced basal‑plane conductivity and active sites, but reverts to 2H unless stabilized</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-3">In situ Raman/XRD tracking in lithium‑intercalated MoS2 shows 2H→1T’ phase transitions nucleate heterogeneously and proceed electrochemically, evidencing a voltage‑controlled phase pathway that doping can tune</cite>.

1) Why phase stabilization dominates the causal chain
- Kinetic/structural bottleneck: 1T‑MoS2 is metallic and kinetically unstable; ambient or electrolyte conditions favor reversion to semiconducting 2H, suppressing conductivity and basal‑plane activity. Thus, unlocking 1T’s full catalytic potential requires suppressing phase transitions. <cite id="48f70a5a-2">Phase engineering from 2H to 1T is considered the most effective strategy for regulating electronic properties and increasing active sites in MoS2 HER</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">The 1T polytype, while offering higher basal‑plane activity and conductivity, can revert to 2H; stabilization is necessary for durable performance</cite>.
- Direct dopant–structure coupling: Multiple dopants establish covalent anchoring with the chalcogen lattice that physically locks 1T motifs and hinders reversion. <cite id="48f70a5a-3">Ni doping forms Ni–S bonds that induce S atom slip and stabilize the 1T structure, with improved HER metrics</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Re acts as an electron donor and favors local transformation to 1T; Re‑doping stabilizes the 1T phase and supports long‑term shelf and operational stability</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-0">Ru substitution (single atoms, nanoparticles) promotes 2H→1T transition and yields high HER activity; proposed mechanisms include Ru‑induced sulfur vacancy formation and strong Ru–S bonding that drives phase conversion; DFT+experiments aim to resolve mechanism</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Co/Ni co‑doping provides abundant electrons for Mo atoms, leading to phase transition to 1T and excellent alkaline HER</cite>.
- Electrochemical proof: Stabilized doped 1T materials exhibit superior durability compared to undoped 1T or purely intercalated systems that lack dopant‑driven covalent anchoring. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Undoped 1T often reverts to 2H; Re‑doped 1T remains stable under HER and on shelf</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Ni‑modified 1T‑MoS2 delivered η50≈187 mV and stable 28‑hour performance, attributed to conductivity increase and active‑site regulation</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">S‑vacancy/intercalated 1T‑MoS2 achieved 158 mV at 10 mA cm−2 and Tafel 74.5 mV dec−1 with notable stability; charge redistribution and Mo–Mo activation lowered ΔGH* for HER</cite>.

2) Electronic structure modification as the proximate performance driver once 1T is stabilized
- Electron doping and conductivity: Once 1T is locked in by dopants, electron donation increases states near EF, boosts carrier density, and enhances interlayer conductivity, improving mass/charge transport to basal‑plane active sites. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Re acts as an n‑type donor, enhancing conductivity and creating basal‑plane 1T active sites that otherwise revert</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Ni modification significantly enhanced conductivity and regulated surface electron density, increasing active sites</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Co/Ni co‑doping induced 1T with abundant electrons for Mo atoms and excellent HER</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-0">S‑rich intercalation in 1T‑MoS2 sustained stability for months and activated basal planes with ΔGH*≈0.06 eV</cite>.
- Adsorption thermodynamics and S‑Sheffield descriptors: Charge transfer and lattice covalency shifts alter d‑band interactions and apparent adsorption energies, optimizing HER overpotentials. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Electronic states of S‑vacancy 1T‑MoS2 show charge redistribution with activated Mo–Mo bonds and optimal ΔGH* for HER, correlating with lower overpotentials and Tafel slopes</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-1">Ru‑doped MoS2 exhibits enhanced HER; DFT and experiments were combined to probe Ru‑induced 2H→1T transitions and strong Ru–H relevant bond energetics, supporting optimized adsorption thermodynamics</cite>.
- Polymorph comparisons underscore the role of metallic 1T conductivity: Even when structure is held fixed, the metallic 1T phase outperforms 2H for HER, consistent with transport and basal‑plane activity gains once stabilized. <cite id="84d915fc-2">The 3R phase outperforms 2H for HER and is comparable to exfoliated 1T in MoS2, highlighting metallic phase conductivity/active‑site availability</cite>.

3) Defect engineering as a downstream lever and complementary pathway
- S‑vacancies and edges: Doping and intercalation often co‑produce sulfur vacancies and edge/basal reconstructions that densify active sites and tune adsorption. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Chemical etching of intercalated 1T‑MoS2 to create S‑vacancies delivered η10≈158 mV and Tafel 74.5 mV dec−1; electronic states showed charge redistribution and Mo–Mo activation lowering ΔGH*</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-3">Ni doping induces S slip and stabilizes 1T, while also increasing active sites and electron density</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-0">Li intercalation promotes HER on H‑phase MoS2, with reactivity defined by T‑like S sites; intercalation can be a route to design basal‑plane activity</cite>.

4) Comparative dominance and contingencies
- Primary causal lever: Across multiple dopants, the consistent causal enabler is stabilization of the 1T phase. - Trade‑offs and design space: Not all dopants are equal; Ni and Re generally stabilize 1T robustly and improve HER, whereas some dopants (e.g., Mn, Fe) underperform, suggesting dopant choice tunes covalency and lattice stability. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Systematic ion modification ranked Ni>Co>1T>others; Ni gave η50=187 mV and ~28 h stability</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">The authors propose that optimal Ni modification enhances conductivity and regulates surface electron density</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Re doping stabilizes 1T and delivers long‑term stability under HER</cite>. Ion intercalation (K/Li) can stabilize 1T and activate basal planes, but alkali durability can be limited, making co‑stabilization via covalent dopants attractive. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Alkali metals stabilize 1T but suffer from poor durability; Re doping improves operational stability</cite>.

5) Integrative evidence from operando and theory
- Operando phase control: In situ Raman and XRD establish that 2H↔1T conversion is voltage/defect controlled and can be leveraged by heterointerfaces and doping to maintain 1T under catalysis. <cite id="84d915fc-3">Nucleation and growth of 1T domains are observed under potential, with distinct Raman signatures for 2H and 1T’</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-4">Encapsulation with graphene/hBN changes interfacial electron doping required for the transition, showing that heterointerfaces tune the voltage needed to induce 2H→1T</cite>.
- Theory + experiment convergence: DFT and electrocatalysis measurements tie Ru/Ni/Co–S bonding to phase conversion and optimized adsorption energetics, resolving earlier controversies by showing multiple pathways (vacancy formation vs direct covalent anchoring) that converge on stabilized 1T with improved ΔGH*. <cite id="84d915fc-0">Ru can induce sulfur vacancies and form strong Ru–S bonds promoting 2H→1T, with DFT+experiment used to reconcile competing mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-1">Supporting data (XRD, XPS, CV) and performance comparisons accompany Ru‑doped MoS2 studies</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Co/Ni co‑doping provides abundant electrons to Mo for phase transition; S‑vacancy engineering improves ΔGH* and HER</cite>.

6) Practical implications for design and attribution
- Attribution test: If a doped 1T catalyst reverts to 2H under operation, activity loss should map to phase loss and increased resistance; if phase is stabilized (e.g., by strong M–S anchoring), activity should remain or improve. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">1T’s enhanced conductivity and basal sites are retained when stabilized by Re; stabilized 1T retains shelf and HER stability</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-3">Ni–S anchoring stabilizes 1T and improves HER metrics</cite>.
- Dominance assessment: Among equal‑structure comparators, stabilized doped 1T consistently outperforms undoped 1T and intercalated systems that lack covalent anchoring, indicating stabilization as the dominant causal factor with electronic/defect tuning as amplifiers. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Ni‑modified 1T outperformed Co/Fe/Cu/Mn systems and undoped 1T, with conductivity/electron density/active‑site changes proposed</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">Intercalated/S‑vacancy 1T improved η and Tafel and showed ΔGH* optimization, but dopant stabilization adds durability</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Re‑doped 1T maintains long lifetimes where undoped 1T reverts, underscoring stabilization dominance</cite>.

Conclusion
The weight of evidence indicates that transition‑metal doping causally dominates electrochemical gains in 1T‑MoS2 by stabilizing the 1T polytype through covalent M–S anchoring and electron doping, which together suppress phase reversion and unlock higher conductivity and basal‑plane active‑site availability; electronic‑structure tuning and defect engineering (e.g., S‑vacancies) are proximate, mechanism‑amplifying changes that optimize adsorption thermodynamics and active‑site density, explaining the observed overpotential and Tafel improvements. <cite id="48f70a5a-0">Dopant‑induced regulation of conductivity, electron density, and active‑site number improves η and stability, ranking Ni first among tested ions</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-3">Ni–S covalent bonding induces S slip and stabilizes 1T with improved overpotential and Tafel</cite>. <cite id="6661d4ba-4">Re doping both stabilizes 1T and enhances charge transfer, delivering long‑term HER stability</cite>. <cite id="48f70a5a-1">S‑vacancy/intercalated 1T shows charge‑redistribution and ΔGH* optimization linked to lower η and improved kinetics</cite>. <cite id="84d915fc-3">Operando Raman/XRD shows 2H↔1T dynamics under potential, and heterointerfaces/dopants tune electron doping and transition voltages, reinforcing phase‑stabilization causality</cite>. Title: Recent progress of MoS2 for photocatalytic and electrocatalytic hydrogen generation—A review
Snippet: Recently, atom intercalation in MoS2 has been confirmed to stabilize MoS2's phase structure. For instance, Ekspong et al. [91] developed sulfur-rich intercalated 1T-MoS2 on graphitic nanoribbons with an S:Mo ratio of ~2.3:1, which sustained its stability for several months. Title: The effects of polymorphism and lithium intercalation on the hydrogen evolution reaction for the basal planes of MoS2.
Snippet: The activity of Li-intercalated MoS2 phases for the hydrogen evolution reaction is investigated using density functional theory. The most stable semiconducting 2H phase, the metallic 1T' phase, and a polymorphous surface composed of alternating H and T' phases (1T″) are investigated. The local structure of the MoS2 surface is found to define its reactivity. In all cases, active sites for the hydrogen evolution process are restricted to T-like sulphur sites. Li-intercalation is found to promote hydrogen evolution reaction reactivity for the H phase whilst having little effect on the T phase. While improved compared to the non-intercalated phase, the Li-intercalated H phase MoS2 still has minimal activity for the hydrogen evolution reaction. The same effect of intercalation is also found for another transition metal dichalcogenide, MoSe2. The ability to improve reactivity in this way makes ion intercalation a promising space for designing new 2D catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction.

In particular, Re-doped MoS2 nanomaterials (RexMo1-xS2) have shown remarkable improvement on the HER activity over MoS2 nanocatalysts [15][16][17][18].The n-type Re dopant not only acts as an electron donor, but also favors local transformation to 1T-MoS2, while both effects contribute to improved HER performance [19][20][21][22].Although the 1T-MoS2 polytype provides enhanced conductivity and basal-plane HER active sites [11,23], it is a metastable phase which can revert to the 2H phase.Nevertheless, Re-doping stabilizes the 1T phase and 1T-RexMo1-xS2 has shown long lifetimes on the shelf and stability under HER conditions [15,17].In comparison, alkali metals can also stabilize 1T-MoS2 nanocatalysts, but they are known to suffer from poor durability [22,24].Indeed, beyond the HER activity, the appeal of MoS2-based nanocatalysts relies on the high stability during operation.

snippet.text: The activity of Li-intercalated MoS2 phases for the hydrogen evolution reaction is investigated using density functional theory. The most stable semiconducting 2H phase, the metallic 1T' phase, and a polymorphous surface composed of alternating H and T' phases (1T″) are investigated. documents.snippet:
Moreover, phase junctions within the same materials have been demonstrated as a promising approach due to the unique benefits of robust coupling, high electron affinity, and the absence of foreign elements. For instance, Cai and coworkers demonstrated that the incorporation of 25% 1T-MoS 2 into 2H-MoS 2 nanosheets resulted in a ten-fold increase in electron concentration [27]. Most recently, we have reported a significant enhancement in photocatalytic hydrogen evolution through improving the conductivity of ZnIn 2 S 4 by the incorporation of the 2H@1T-MoS 2 phase [28]. However, the mechanism of the MoS 2 transformation from 2H to 1T is still unclear, and the influence of the phase transformation of MoS 2 on the HER activity also requires in-depth research. 

Ruthenium (Ru) doping has been reported to promote the phase transformation of MoS 2 from 2H to 1T and shows the high HER activity. Moreover, the bond energy of Ru-H is approximately 65 kcal mol −1 , equivalent to the energy of Pt-H bond [29][30][31]. In previous studies, Ru materials including single atoms, nanoparticles, and clusters, have been demonstrated to possess high HER performances [32][33][34][35]. Zhang et al. have reported that MoS 2 -based electrocatalysts loaded with the single-atom Ru exhibit the significantly enhanced HER activity due to the 2H-to-1T phase transition [36]. The reason for phase transition is owing to the introduction of sulfur vacancies by Ru single-atom doping. Recently, Wang and co-workers believed that single-atom Ru substitution for the Mo atom in MoS 2 resulted in the 2H-to-1T phase transition, which makes the Ru-MoS 2 electrocatalysts have superb HER performances [37]. However, there is still controversy over the mechanism of the MoS 2 transformation from 2H to 1T through the introduction of Ru. It is necessary to reveal the mechanism through the combination of theoretical calculation and experimental study. 

In this work, we employed the DFT calculation and experiments to study the electrocatalytic HER activity on Ru-doped MoS 2 catalysts.
